p:
No. Definitely we don't want to lose any more and we know how that impacts the local neighborhoods and the communities, and so hopefully that won't happen. And I know that our Health Chair, Chair Schulman, as well as a Health and Hospitals Chair, Mercedes Narcisse, are very attuned to this issue as well.

And I know that you had announced pilots at certain H and H ER locations to improve the turnaround times, and so do you have any updates on that and is that something you're looking to expand?

Yeah. So, that was called the Hospital Liaison Officer Pilot, and that pilot is still ongoing. We're going to be exploring lots of different things, I would say, over the next few years. We have to continue to also have these conversations within the hospitals themselves and work with our partners in the emergency room, the administrators, to come up with creative ways to transfer a patient from the EMS crew to the hospital themselves so that we can expedite our exit from the hospital. So as of right now, those programs are still ongoing and they are, you know, they're not in all hospitals. They're in certain hospitals.
And if you could remind me, when did it start, the pilot program, and how long is it for?
I believe it was 2024. Chief Miano?
(INAUDIBLE)
November 2024.
Okay. Thank you. And in terms of the Chief Savings Officers, have you designated a Chief Savings Officer or equivalent position as proposed by the Mayor to identify some of the cost savings?
Yes, I have. I've identified a very awesome Chief Savings Officer, and this is Commissioner Christoff sitting right next to me.

Great. And what percentage of your time is sort of dedicated to looking, taking a deeper dive and looking into the savings initiatives versus other administrative duties, and what budgetary authority does the officer have to implement in terms of cost reduction measures without requiring approval from OMB or other external entities?

Yeah. I mean, it is certainly taking up a lot of my time as we're moving towards the submission of the Chief Savings Officer reports. It's something me and my team are very focused on. You know, because I am also the Deputy Commissioner for Management and Budget, I

do have the authority within the Department to implement savings measures as we identify them.

Okay. That's great. And what specific cost saving targets or benchmarks have been established for FY27 and what percentage reduction in operating expenses or improvement in operational efficiency do these targets represent?

So, the targets are one and a half percent in the current year and two and a half percent in the outyears. Those percentages are off of our City tax levy budget. So, for us, the sort of annual going forward is around 54 million.

Okay. And what sort of, just out of curiosity, what type of cost savings are, you know, if you could give us buckets. I mean, obviously, I know the reports are not due yet, but what are some of the things that you all are looking at?

So, we're still in the process of finalizing what the recommendations will be, and they will have to be, you know, internally vetted as we move forward with

the process. We do anticipate that the savings will be reflected in the executive budget. And certainly, you know, we're looking for efficiencies and things that don't impact emergency services.

Exactly. I think that's key too. And what is, you know, and I know this is ongoing, but if you, for future reference, if you could note, if you could report back what the projected annual savings from each of the initiatives expressed are in terms of dollar amount as well as percentage of the total agency's budget, that would be great. And if you are able to answer, have any of these savings been realized in reduced budget requests, or have they been redirected to address other agency priorities?

So, there certainly are, you know, simpler components of our savings as we're identifying them, you know, assuming they're non-controversial, there are no negative repercussions to doing so. We are moving forward and locking in those savings as soon as we possibly can,

but the intent is for them to go towards the executive budget savings.

Got it. Okay. And lastly, how does FDNY ensure the cost savings measures pursued by yourself do not compromise service quality, public safety, as you mentioned, or regulatory compliance, and what percentage of proposed saving initiatives have been rejected due to potential negative impacts on operations as well? Because as you mentioned, I think that's important to look at, because we want to make sure that you're still able to do all the things that you need to do. And so if you could speak a little bit to that, that would be great.

Yeah, the savings process isn't being done, you know, unilaterally by myself. So, there have been lots of conversations with bureau heads throughout the Department and our senior leadership team to make sure that our savings proposals won't negatively impact operations. Ultimately, our final submission will get signed off on by the Fire Commissioner and will be reviewed by City Hall and OMB as well.
Great. Thank you. That's it. Thank you so much again for being here. And thank you, Chair.

Thank you. I just want to do a couple of follow-ups with the Chief Savings Officer. I know that the position is to go in and see where there can be, you know, monies that can be better spent or perhaps taken from. The Fire Department hasn't received any new money in the four years that I've been the Chair, and not before. It's always been flatlined. And you made references to initiatives. What kind of initiatives? Would you, could you describe them better, more, explain them? What type of initiatives you think money can be taken from?

So, we're certainly looking at everything. I mean, I think the actual final initiatives won't be ready until later this month, and we anticipate talking through them in detail as part of the executive budget process. But our north star in this whole process is making sure we're not negatively impacting emergency operations. So, we're looking for, you know, efficiencies that

don't do that, that don't negatively impact on our first responders.

Because in the last three budget cycles that I've been Chair, we've asked for 1 billion dollars for the Fire Department, not for any money to be taken from the Fire Department. They've been working on a baseline. And in fact, when I had a conversation with the First Deputy Mayor and the Director of OMB, I asked that the Fire Department be exempt from any type of, any type of removal of any of their funding and exempt from having a Chief Savings Officer. But I guess that fell on deaf ears. But, okay. So, the FY27 preliminary budget totals 2.646 billion, an increase of 24.6 million from the FY26 adopted budget. The headcount includes, as I said in my statement, 17,566 positions. Key increases include fire extinguishment, emergency response, fire prevention, and fire investigation. The FY27 budget totals 2.46 billion, up 24.6 million from FY26. What percentage has the FDNY's budget grown over the past 10 fiscal years adjusted for inflation?

So, the comparison point for that would be the preliminary

budget for FY17, which was released in January of 2016. That was 1.9 billion dollars. If you adjust that for inflation using CPI, that would be 2.62 billion today. That's actually very close to the budget for FY27, which is about 26 million above that inflation adjusted number. So, our budget has gone up by about 1 percent above inflation.

Right. So, you're agreeing that the Fire Department hasn't really gone over their budget. They actually are operating, they're operating with a budget that's never been increased. They're continuing to operate, continuing to put out fires, continuing to send their EMS trucks out, continuing to do the job to keep the people of this city safe without receiving one extra penny from the City of New York. So, I'm glad we agree about that. What percentage of the FDNY's budget is allocated to personal services versus OTPS, other than personal services?
So, our PS budget is approximately 90 percent of our overall budget. So, in FY27, PS is 2.396 billion, and OTPS is 249.8 million.

Okay. And fire extinguishment, emergency responses, they represent 1.844 billion, or 69.7 percent of the budget. And that's, according to what we saw, that's up 21.5 million. What drove the increase, and what percentage is for salary increases versus operational enhancements?

So, none of the increase is tied to operational enhancements. It's related to the PS adjustment that was provided for in the preliminary budget that included, you know, Department-wide 57 million in FY27. The purpose of that was really to align the budget with anticipated spending, and that's what that is.
I didn't catch the last, to align the budget with?
With anticipated spending.

With anticipated spending, okay. And fire prevention increased 6.9 million, 13.8 percent, to 56.7 million. What percentage of this increase is for additional

inspector positions versus other fire prevention initiatives?

So, that increase is also primarily related to the PS adjustment that was provided for in the preliminary budget. So, that 57 million that was given Department-wide includes 6.5 million that went into (INAUDIBLE) for fire prevention.
And the emergency medical services is budgeted for 416.8 million, down 2.9 million. Given worsening EMS response times, why was the EMS budget decreased, and what operational impacts did this have?

So, that decrease is primarily driven by the transfer of B-HEARD funding to H and H that was done as part of the November plan under the former administration. We anticipate that that funding will be transferred back in a future plan.

I'm just going to hold for a moment because Council Member Paladino has another place to go, and she just has two questions that she'd like to ask. So, I'm going to just yield

to Council Member Paladino for questions, and then I'll come back to my questioning.
Good morning. Can you hear me?
Yes.

Yes? Okay. I'm interested to know, you know, my office, since Fiscal Year '23, we funded 1.2 million for generators for one firehouse; in '24, another 1.2 million for another generator; in '25, we fully funded an ambulance simulator at 300,000 dollars; and in '26, we just did an EMS 53 vehicle for another 323,000 dollars. It's over 3 million. My question is, how, and is it true that after 9/11, the State required these firehouses to have these new updated generators, and how do we go about getting this work done? I mean, this has been going on since 2023. My firehouses need them. They are truly in need. Also, another question, the firehouses are in, I visit all the time, and my firehouses, of which I have four, are, really need renovation terribly. Is there any way we're going to be able to get you guys what you need, most importantly with your ambulances and your EMS vehicles and your

generators? The renovation is like the topping on a cupcake, but still just the same. These guys practically live there. So, and they're in dire need. Can you help me out with that?

Yes. And thank you for the support that you've given us. Very much appreciated. As we start to move forward, you know, it's important, I'll just level set us here, and then I'll tell you where we're at with some of the repairs. This Fire Department is the most recognized fire department in the world. This patch will be recognized anywhere in the world, and it's primarily because we've been around 160 years. We're a staple of New York City and the greatest Fire Department in the world. But a lot of our buildings are about a century old now. We've been around 160 years, and a lot of our buildings are about 100 years or more. So, yes, these buildings are in states of needing repair, and we certainly appreciate all the assistance that we get from the Committee and the Council Members. So, when we're taking this into account, and we have many, many facilities, they all need some sort of repair at some point. So, the way we manage

this generally is we'll take a look at the order, right, the actual complaint, what it is that needs repair, and we prioritize them. The most urgent or the most dangerous ones we address first. As a complaint comes in, we'll send our fleet team out to do an assessment and to prioritize whether this is something that is urgent or dangerous, or if it's something that we can handle in-house. If it's something that is dangerous or urgent we can handle in-house, we do right away. We get our facilities team over there to fix it. If it's something we can't handle, we'll vendor that out. But we do have to work in order of urgency, because there are so many repairs that need to be done. The capital budget that we have, about half of our capital budget is for facility repair. If we were able to get unlimited money for these repairs, we still would not be able to handle all the repairs at once. Part of the issue that exists is as we start to repair some of these houses, and we will, we certainly will continue to do that work, we have to relocate the resource that is housed in that area, in that particular firehouse or EMS station, and we can't move too many of them, because that ends up

leaving areas of our city that don't have coverage and response coverage so we're limited by the amount of resources that we can move out at one time, and we're certainly limited by the number of people who can do the repairs. So, I think that's where we are. We're just as interested in making these repairs as quickly as possible, and I do believe that we're in a place where we're doing that. And should anybody have anything urgent, they should be sure to put that order in so that we could get our facilities team out there to take a look at it.

Commissioner, I know what the Council Member is asking also, because we will go much deeper, Council Member, as the hearing goes along into the condition of our firehouses. But I mean, we all get very frustrated, because the money that we do appropriate, taxpayer dollars to give generators, bathrooms, kitchens, locker rooms, you know, oftentimes gets cogged up in procurement. So, you know, what we would really, if anyone can answer the question, is why there is always a backup that money from '21 or '20, I'm sorry, 2022, '23, and '24 and '25. Now we're into '27, and we're still not

seeing generators that were paid for in previous years.

Yes. I understand the frustration. And do you want to speak? I think Jeremy Brooks? So, our facilities -- do you want to come up and address some of these questions about generators and repairs? Just introduce yourself. Hello. Sorry. So --
Can we swear you in for a second, right? Can you just state your name for the record and I could swear you in.
Sorry. Jeremy Brooks.
Can you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth and to answer honestly to Council Member questions.
Yes.
You may go ahead. Thank you so much.

Thanks. So, in regards to generators, approximately 70 percent of

our locations currently have emergency generator backup. It's one of our priorities to have every one of our locations to have a generator backup. We've been doing this program, like you said, probably since around 2001. So about 70 percent of our locations do have a generator. When we do get the money from City Council for various projects, and we are greatly thankful because that helps us out tremendously for a lot of our work, for a generator, it usually takes about 18 months to get the project completed, from once we get the money to doing design, construction so it does take a little time to actually get a project from start to finish. It is a slow process. I wish there were some things we could do to expedite, but it's just permitting, funding. But again, we greatly appreciate everything that everyone has given us throughout the years.

So, what kind of program do you use? And do you find that after you go through the 18 months of what you need to do, are you finding that there's a problem at OMB with releasing the money for these items?

I don't think it's a problem with funding. I think just sometimes

there's a lot of permitting process. There's a lot of sign-offs from different agencies, Landmarks, Public Design Commission that have to go through Department of Buildings. That is just unfortunately to do a lot of work on any City building or even public building, it's a slow process.
Right. But once it reaches OMB, do you have an issue with OMB releasing the funds after all those permits and all the processes are in place? Is there a problem with OMB?
I think we have a pretty good relationship with OMB. They know what our initiatives are and what our priorities are, and we have continuous meetings with them weekly about projects.

Would you mind checking on the, and I can have them written out for you, just Council Member Paladino, because she brought up her initiatives and see where they are in the pipeline and if they are at OMB, then possibly we can be helpful --
Of course.
-- in helping that get out. We'll get that information to you both.
Sure. Thank you.

Thank you. I just want to come back to Chief Savings Officer. Has the FDNY designated, well, obviously they have. Is there an equivalent position as proposed by Mayor Mamdani to identify operational efficiencies and cost-saving opportunities and what percentage of the position's time is dedicated solely to savings initiatives versus other administrative duties? And what budgetary authority do you have to implement cost-reduction measures without requiring approval from OMB or external entities?

Yes. So, certainly a high percentage of my time has been focused on working on the savings proposals since the announcement was made and now through the development of my final recommendations. You know, as the Deputy Commissioner for Management and Budget within the Department, I do already have authority internally to execute on these savings proposals.

As you can see, we're very concerned that you're going to take money from

the FDNY and we cannot have that happen. We really can't. Okay. Well, let's talk about headcount. So, in FY27, budget included 17,566 positions, 11,294 were uniformed, 6,272 were civilian. By what percentage has FDNY's total headcount changed over the past five fiscal years?

So, the January 2021 budget for FY22, which is the comparison point from five years ago, was 17,288 positions. That breaks down as 10,945 uniform and 6,343 civilian. That includes EMS, which is 278 more than the FY27 budget.
Okay. And we have civilian positions decreased by 44 from FY26. So, you don't agree with that?

So, that 44 for civilian positions, so EMS is reflected as civilian in all the published budget documents, and that 44 is the decrease tied to the B-HEARD transfer, which we do anticipate will be reversed in a future plan.

This is just me thinking out loud, but it's interesting that EMS

would be considered civilian when they are recognized by law as a member of emergency service so that's interesting. We're going to have to look into that. What is the current vacancy rate for uniformed versus civilian positions? Would you say they're up, right?

Yes. So, on the uniform side, so this is like firefighter and, you know, fire officers. Our current budgeted number of positions is 11,294, and our actuals are 11,092 so we have 202 vacancies. That's a 1.8 percent vacancy rate. On the EMS side, our budgeted number is 4,499, and our actuals are 4,174 so that's 325 vacancies, which is a 7.2 percent vacancy rate. I will note that that's comparing actuals on payroll. The number of people in the field is obviously less than that, because the payroll actuals include folks who are still in training. And then on the civilian, non-EMS side, our budget is 1,784, and our actuals are 1,795. We're actually 11 above budgeted headcount.

Okay. What is the total cost impact of recent collective bargaining agreements of FDNY's FY27 budget expressed, and

please express, as a dollar amount and percentage of the budget growth?
So, I don't actually believe that any of our major unions have collective bargaining increases that have been agreed to yet that impact FY27.
So, my next question would have been, what percentage of FDNY's budget growth over the next three years is driven by contractual wage increases versus new programs?

None of it yet. So, the City budgets for anticipated collective bargaining increases centrally in the labor reserve, so that's where you would see that funding, which OMB can speak to and, as the agreements get settled, that funding is transferred into agency budgets.

Okay. I had asked earlier about what other initiatives you could take from to give to the Fire Department, and you could take money from other initiatives. I really would just like one initiative, what have you, in the time you've spent, what have you come up with that can be utilized to better fund the FDNY?

So, those are still being worked through, but, you know, as directed by the Mayor, one area we're certainly looking at is, you know, payments that we make to vendors, also just looking for efficiencies and potential rate reductions.
Do you think that the FDNY would benefit from a design-build approach to capital improvements?
Sure. Yes.

Okay. Let's talk about overtime. I'm going to talk about overtime, and then I'm going to yield to my Colleagues who are here, and I see we've been joined by Pierina Sanchez, Council Member Sanchez. What is the total budgeted overtime for FDNY in '27, and what percentage of the total budget does this represent?
So, the total budgeted overtime in FY27 is 472.5 million dollars. That's about 18 percent of our budget.
How does this compare to '26 and '25 budgeted overtime expressed as percentage changes?
So, FY26 budgeted overtime is 546.9 million, so that's about 16 percent higher than the '27 amount. In FY25, actual overtime spending is 569.1 million, about 20 percent above '27 levels.
And what is the actual overtime spending year-to-date, and what percentage of the budgeted overtime does that represent?
So, year-to-date through February '26, we spent about 380 million. That is about 69 percent of the FY26 budgeted overtime.
Okay. And in firefighter overtime, what is the budgeted firefighter overtime? It was 381 million in FY25. And what percentage of the total FDNY overtime does this present?
So, we don't budget overtime by title. But if you're looking at uniformed overtime, and you are looking for FY25 actuals, we spent 477.8 million in uniformed overtime.
And for EMS overtime, what is the budgeted EMS overtime, and what percentage of the total EMS budget does this represent?
So, FY26 budgeted EMS overtime is 68.6 million. And that is about 17 percent of the total EMS PS budget.
Okay. I will now yield to Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Commissioner. Thank you for being here today. District 30 is proud to be a district with one of the largest populations of active and retired FDNY members in the city, including firefighters, EMTs, and civilian employees. Many families in our community have deep ties to the Department and have served the people of New York for generations. As we approach the 25th anniversary of September 11th, this September, it is especially important that we ensure our firehouses are properly supported, that our firefighters and EMS members have the resources they need to do their jobs, and that the legacy of those who have made the ultimate sacrifice is honored appropriately. One firehouse in my District, Squad

288 and Hazmat 1 in Maspeth, lost 19 firefighters on September 11th, and is the greatest loss from any single FDNY firehouse that day. My office has also been discussing an idea related to the upcoming anniversary about recognizing FDNY and NYPD members who died on September 11th through updated street sign designations, and I will be asking about that shortly. With that in mind, I want to ask a few questions about firehouse capital planning and EMS staffing and several initiatives that are important to both to my District and to the City. My first question is a firehouse capital funding. In the past, many firehouse capital projects across the city have appeared in the capital plan at roughly 1.2 million, regardless of the scope of work, whether the project involves a kitchen renovation, bathroom upgrade, generator or installation, or other infrastructure improvements, the amount is always 1.2 million. Can you explain why these projects have historically appeared with the same funding amount? And then I have a follow-up.

I mean, obviously the costs per location and per project do

differ. I mean, averages are used when coming up with some of those estimates. I think it's just coincidence that the totals tend to be similar.

I was the former Council Member Robert Holden's Budget Director, so I see 1.2 million everywhere we do capital projects, and I always wanted to ask that. Okay. My next question. Is that figure based on a detailed engineering estimate, or is it being used as a placeholder until the scope of work is finalized?
So, it depends on what stage of the process that we are. Certainly, at the very beginning, it's based on average historical costs, and, you know, it gets refined as the project moves forward.

Okay. Thank you. All right. My next question is regarding landmarking the Maspeth Firehouse at Squad 288 Hazmat 1. My predecessor, Council Member Robert Holden, had been advocating for years to landmark the Squad 288 and Hazmat 1 Firehouse in Maspeth. As I mentioned earlier, that firehouse lost 19 firefighters on September 11th, the greatest loss from any single

FDNY firehouse that day. Given the historic significance of the facility and the sacrifice associated with it, we need the FDNY to step in and support landmark designation of that firehouse. Would the Department work with the Landmark Preservation Commission and the City Council to ensure this site receives the recognition and the protection it deserves?

Thank you for that. You know, September 11th was a very difficult day for our Department. We remember and mourn the loss every day of the people that we lost down there. I know how incredibly important that is. We were certainly engaged in a conversation regarding this topic.

Okay. Thank you, thank you. My next question is regarding the 25th anniversary of 9/11 Memorial Street Sign Initiative. This September marks the 25th anniversary of September 11th, and my office recently met with the Department of Transportation to discuss an idea that many families and first responders believe would be meaningful. In the immediate aftermath of September

11th, hundreds of streets across the city were co-named for those who died in attacks. At the time, all of those honorary street signs were installed in green, regardless of whether the (TIMER CHIME) individual was a firefighter, police officer, or civilian. Today, however, the city uses a different system. Red signs are used for FDNY, blue signs are used for NYPD. Okay, can I have more time? I'm almost done, yeah. Green signs are used for civilians. Our idea is simple. For the FDNY and NYPD members who died in September 11th, we believe those existing green signs should be replaced with the appropriate red or blue sign so that it is immediately clear to residents and visitors that the individual honor was a firefighter or police officers who died in the line of duty. Would FDNY support working with the Council and the Department of Transportation to help advance this initiative ahead of the 25th anniversary? Thank you.
Yes.
Yes. Thank you. That's it. I'm done with my questions. Thank you. Thank you.

And Commissioner, just for clarity, because it really kind of stuck in my craw about EMS being considered civilian, and I know what my opinion is about EMS, and I know how I view them, and I know how the law views them as members of uniformed service, and I also know how you view them, but I'd just like that to be said for the record.

Yeah. So, you know, this particular issue is an issue between OLR and the unions, but I can tell you that in the Fire Department, they're all uniformed workers, and when 9-1-1 is called, the question you get is police, fire, or EMS. You don't get police, fire, or the civilians that hang out with us. So, you know, I would love to see this topic work itself out between the unions, OLR, and the City.
Thank you. Council Member Schulman.

Thank you very much, Chair. And, yeah, I was going to ask you the same thing about uniform and civilian, because I consider EMS uniform as well, and just for the record, I used to work at the Emergency Medical

Service, and the Commissioner and I know each other a very long time, and I actually worked there during the merger. I was in the leadership of the administration there, so I have a few questions. One is about, I just want to delve a little bit deeper on the questions asked by the Chair around the overtime. Do you have, because in previous years you've overspent your overtime funds, so is there a plan in place to rein in overtime because that's also a place for savings as well.

Yes. So, we monitor overtime very closely, and we actually have regular monthly meetings with OMB and City Hall to talk about our overtime spending and our overtime projections. You know, there were several Mayoral Directives on overtime in the former Administration, and we have been working towards making progress on reducing overtime. It gets a little complicated when you're looking at dollars because collective bargaining increases and just changes in where folks are in their tenure do impact those? But if you look at overtime hours from FY23 to FY25, we actually did see a 2 percent decrease, which is showing the impact of the various measures we've put into place. When

you're looking at our overtime, the overwhelming majority of it is tied to staffing fire companies. So, we operate on a fixed post system, which means that at the start of every tour, we need to make sure we have the right number of fire personnel available. Otherwise, the company can't be in service, and overtime is used to fill those gaps. And as we were talking about earlier, when we were talking about our headcount, we're still under budgeted headcount on the fire operation side. So, the single most impactful thing that we can do to control overtime spending is to continue to work to get back up to headcount by hiring additional firefighters.

Whatever we can do to be helpful there. And one of the things that the Council was looking at maybe is like an overtime reduction plan. I mean, the NYPD has similar issues as a uniformed service. And also, what are your headcount targets for '27, for Fiscal Year '27.
So, I mean, we are continuing to process firefighter classes. I'm not sure if you want the class information or the overall headcount.
Overall headcount target.
Yes. So, our authorized headcount on the uniform side is 11,294. We're actually at 11,092. So, we're 202 under.
Is that on both sides, the EMS and the FDNY or just FDNY?
So that's fire.
Okay.

On the EMS side, our authorized headcount is 4,499, and we are actually at 4,174. So, we're 325 under budgeted headcount. And as I mentioned before, it is an even greater deficit in the field because that payroll headcount does count folks who are still in training.

Okay. The other thing, too, I know we've spent a little bit of time on the response times. Particularly, I'm focused on EMS. I know it's gone up to some degree. When I was in EMS many, many years ago, the targeted response time was eight minutes, and so I just want to know

where we, you know, what the thinking is in terms of moving ahead in terms of lowering the response time.
Yeah, eight minutes, huh? What? Eight minutes.
It was eight minutes. And we met it pretty much, and that was during -- there was a lot going on then. Go ahead.

Yes. I remember. So, I just would like to talk a little bit about response times and what that means. And then we'll talk about some solutions, hopefully. So, one of the things that happen in response times is that there are lots of different things that lead into these response times. And when we talk about response times, we talk about picking up the call from 9-1-1 and actually getting to the patient. And there are lots of factors in between that lead to higher (TIMER CHIME) response times. Staffing most certainly is one of the priority concerns here. The fewer ambulances you run, the longer it takes to get an ambulance to an assignment so staffing is a priority, which is why I've come out so strongly in support of parity. This is not just about being fair, but this is about stabilizing an EMS system for New York so we do want

to increase our staff. We want to create an environment where people could come and stay, be a destination itself. They can come and have a long career, help us run ambulances so that we can continue to serve the public. The other thing to note here is one third of the EMS system is made up of our voluntary hospital partners. So, these are private EMS, hospital-based EMS system, right? So, they provide one third of New York City service. The Fire Department provides two thirds. There have been, across the last several years, several places where ambulances were taken out of the 9-1-1 system, right? So, that's fewer ambulances in the system to help us get to those calls. We've had an increase of call volume. So, while our resources are static for the most part, our staffing is low, the call volume has increased, and we've seen a significant increase in call volume. From 2022 to 2025, we've seen about an 18 percent increase in call volume and a 4 percent increase in fire incidents during that period of time. So, we have resources that are either diminishing based on participation, staffing that is much lower than it was, and increasing call volume,

and hospitals that are closing, meaning that we have to go further and we have to wait longer because the hospitals are also in this triage circle where they're going to take the most urgent patient first and make us wait basically until they can triage out our ambulance crew. So, there are a lot of different things that contribute to this. We also, I will note, are in a promotion cycle in EMS. So, over the next year to year and a half, two years, we expect to lose up to 25 percent of the EMS workforce moving from EMS to fire. Again, parity is something that is critical here so that people who love medicine can stay and still be able to afford their lives. So, we're in this cycle right now where things are working against each other, leading to higher response times. There's also congestion in the street, you know, that slows things down, and it slows us down as well. And that is by design. And we know when you slow traffic down, you also save lives so I'm not against that. It is just a fact that it slows us all down. So, things we can do to try to help. Well, we have tried several pilots. I think you

mentioned one earlier and that pilot is still going on. We've tried the paramedic response unit right now.
